claim: The canonical view of neuronal function is that inputs are received by dendrites and somata, become integrated in the somatodendritic compartment and upon reaching a sufficient threshold, generate axonal output with axons emerging from the cell body.
source: The canonical view of neuronal function is that inputs are received by dendrites and somata, become integrated in the somatodendritic compartment and upon reaching a sufficient threshold, generate axonal output with axons emerging from the cell body.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus about neuronal function.

claim: Axons may originate from dendrites.
source: Instead, axons may originate from dendrites.
evidence: This is a factual statement about neuronal anatomy that is supported by the observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The terms 'axon carrying dendrite' (AcD) and 'AcD neurons' have been coined to describe the feature of axons originating from dendrites.
source: The terms 'axon carrying dendrite' (AcD) and 'AcD neurons' have been coined to describe this feature.
evidence: This is a statement about terminology used in the field.

claim: In rodent hippocampus, AcD cells are shown to be functionally 'privileged', since inputs here can circumvent somatic integration and lead to immediate action potential initiation in the axon.
source: In rodent hippocampus, AcD cells are shown to be functionally 'privileged', since inputs here can circumvent somatic integration and lead to immediate action potential initiation in the axon.
evidence: This statement references established findings about the functional properties of AcD cells in rodent hippocampus.

claim: In non-primate mammals, 10–21% of pyramidal cells of layers II–VI had an AcD.
source: We found that in non-primate mammals, 10–21% of pyramidal cells of layers II–VI had an AcD.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in the manuscript from multiple non-primate species.

claim: In macaque and human, the proportion of AcD pyramidal cells was lower than in non-primates and was particularly low for supragranular neurons.
source: In marked contrast, in macaque and human, this proportion was lower and was particularly low for supragranular neurons.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data comparing primate and non-primate species presented in the manuscript.

claim: A comparison of six cortical areas (being sensory, association, and limbic in nature) in three macaques yielded percentages of AcD cells which varied by a factor of 2 between the areas and between the individuals.
source: A comparison of six cortical areas (being sensory, association, and limbic in nature) in three macaques yielded percentages of AcD cells which varied by a factor of 2 between the areas and between the individuals.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 4A and the associated text.

claim: Pyramidal cells in the white matter of postnatal cat and aged human cortex exhibit AcDs at much higher percentages than gray matter pyramidal cells.
source: Unexpectedly, pyramidal cells in the white matter of postnatal cat and aged human cortex exhibit AcDs to much higher percentages.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Tables 2 and 4.

claim: Interneurons assessed in developing cat and adult human cortex had AcDs at type-specific proportions and for some types at much higher percentages than pyramidal cells.
source: In addition, interneurons assessed in developing cat and adult human cortex had AcDs at type-specific proportions and for some types at much higher percentages than pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The axon usually originates from the ventral aspect of the soma, starting with a short axon hillock followed by the axon initial segment (AIS), the electrogenic domain generating the action potential.
source: The axon usually originates from the ventral aspect of the soma, starting with a short axon hillock followed by the axon initial segment (AIS), the electrogenic domain generating the action potential (reviewed by Kole and Brette, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Ramon y Cajal suggested that impulses may bypass the soma and flow directly to the axon.
source: Already Ramon y Cajal suggested that impulses may bypass the soma and flow directly to the axon (reviewed by Triarhou, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Axon carrying dendrites (AcDs) are common in cortical inhibitory interneurons.
source: Axon carrying dendrites (AcDs) are common in cortical inhibitory interneurons (Meyer, 1987; Wahle and Meyer, 1987; Meyer and Wahle, 1988; Höfflin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Upright, inverted, and fusiform pyramidal neurons of supra- and infragranular layers display AcDs in Golgi impregnated or dye-injected cortex from rodents, lagomorphs, ungulates, and carnivores.
source: Furthermore, upright, inverted, and fusiform pyramidal neurons of supra- and infragranular layers display AcDs in Golgi impregnated or dye-injected cortex from rodents, lagomorphs, ungulates, and carnivores (Peters et al., 1968; Smit and Uylings, 1975; van der Loos, 1976; Peters and Kara, 1985; Ferrer et al., 1986a; Ferrer et al., 1986b; Hübener et al., 1990; Reblet et al., 1992; Matsubara et al., 1996; Prieto and Winer, 1999; Mendizabal-Zubiaga et al., 2007; Hamada et al., 2016; Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, axons frequently emerge from basal dendrites.
source: In mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, axons frequently emerge from basal dendrites (Thome et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Multiphoton glutamate uncaging and patch clamp recordings revealed that input to the AcD is more efficient in eliciting an action potential than input onto regular dendrites (non-AcDs).
source: Multiphoton glutamate uncaging and patch clamp recordings revealed that input to the AcD is more efficient in eliciting an action potential than input onto regular dendrites (non-AcDs).
evidence: This statement references findings from previous studies on the functional properties of AcD neurons.

claim: AcDs are intrinsically more excitable, generating dendritic spikes with higher probability and greater strength.
source: AcDs are intrinsically more excitable, generating dendritic spikes with higher probability and greater strength.
evidence: This statement references findings from previous studies on the functional properties of AcD neurons.

claim: Synaptic input onto AcDs generates action potentials with lower thresholds compared to non-AcDs, presumably due to the short electrotonic distance between input and the AIS.
source: Synaptic input onto AcDs generates action potentials with lower thresholds compared to non-AcDs, presumably due to the short electrotonic distance between input and the AIS.
evidence: This statement references findings from previous studies and provides a mechanistic explanation.

claim: The anatomical diversity of axon origins plus the diversity of length and position of the AIS substantially impact the electrical behavior of pyramidal neurons.
source: The anatomical diversity of axon origins plus the diversity of length and position of the AIS substantially impact the electrical behavior of pyramidal neurons (reviewed by Kole and Brette, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: AcDs were generally basal dendrites.
source: Generally, AcDs were basal dendrites.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In gray matter of non-primates, 10–21% of the pyramidal neurons assessed by perpendicular counts through all layers had an AcD.
source: In gray matter of non-primates, 10–21% of the pyramidal neurons assessed by perpendicular counts through all layers had an AcD (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3A and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: In adult macaque, gray matter of only about 3–6% of the pyramidal neurons had an AcD.
source: In adult macaque, gray matter of only about 3–6% of the pyramidal neurons had an AcD (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3A and Table 3.

claim: In human gray matter, the proportion of AcD pyramidal neurons was 1.96% on average.
source: In human gray matter, the proportion of AcD pyramidal neurons was 1.96% on average.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 4.

claim: Non-primate species showed roughly equal proportions of AcD neurons in supra- and infragranular layers, with the range being 10–21%.
source: Non-primate species showed roughly equal proportions of AcD neurons in supra- and infragranular layers. With some individual variability the range was 10–21%.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3B and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: In macaque, infragranular pyramidal cells displayed much higher proportions of AcD cells compared with supragranular pyramidal cells.
source: In contrast, in macaque, the cluster was downshifted along the ordinate due to overall much lower proportions. Furthermore, infragranular pyramidal cells displayed much higher proportions of AcD cells compared with supragranular pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3B and Table 3.

claim: A Mann-Whitney rank sum test of 'all non-primate' versus 'all macaque' percentages of supragranular and infragranular AcD cells, yielded p<0.001 and p<0.001, respectively.
source: A Mann-Whitney rank sum test of 'all non-primate' versus 'all macaque' percentages of supragranular and infragranular AcD cells, yielded p<0.001 and p<0.001, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Apical AcDs were rare, less than 10 were detected among the neurons assessed in adult rat, ferret, and macaque, and none in human material.
source: Apical AcDs (asterisk in C2) were rare, less than 10 were detected among the neurons assessed in adult rat, ferret, and macaque, and none in our human material.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In all cases where apical AcDs were observed, the axon immediately bent down toward the white matter.
source: In all cases, the axon immediately bent down toward the white matter.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In three individuals, the percentages of AcD neurons varied between six cortical areas by about a factor of 2.
source: In three individuals, the percentages of AcD neurons varied between the six areas by about a factor of 2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no recognizable systematic difference in that one of the cortical areas presented with substantially higher or lower percentages of AcD neurons.
source: We could not recognize a systematic difference in that one of the areas presented with substantially higher or lower percentages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Individual percentages of AcD neurons in cat visual cortex varied from 11 to 20%; the interindividual variability was larger than the interareal variability.
source: Also here, individual percentages of AcD neurons varied from 11 to 20%; the interindividual variability was larger than the interareal variability.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no recognizable difference between the visual areas analyzed in cat.
source: There was no recognizable difference between the areas analyzed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The values obtained in cat visual cortex matched those in ferret visual cortex (striate and extrastriate).
source: Moreover, the values obtained in cat visual cortex matched those in ferret visual cortex (striate and extrastriate) (Figure 4B; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: Cells with the shared root configuration according to our criteria have been accepted in recent studies already as AcD neurons.
source: Yet, cells with the shared root configuration according to our criteria have been accepted in recent studies already as AcD neurons (Thome et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The species cluster along the ordinate as already evident in Figure 3B, but scatter widely along the abscissa when plotting AcD versus shared root percentages.
source: In Figure 5A, the species cluster along the ordinate as already evident in Figure 3B. However, in Figure 5A, the species scatter widely along the abscissa.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: There is an absence of a systematic correlation between AcD and the shared root configuration.
source: This suggested an absence of a systematic correlation between AcD and the shared root configuration.
evidence: This is an inference from the data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: If the shared root cells were considered as AcD cells, the proportions of AcD cells increase to some extent in all species analyzed.
source: If the shared root cells were considered as AcD cells, the proportions of AcD cells increase to some extent in all species analyzed.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The interindividual variability of the shared root cells was at a factor of >10 (range of 0.46–5.5% in macaque).
source: The interindividual variability of the shared root cells was at a factor of >10 (range of 0.46–5.5% in macaque), and statistics argued against any biologically significant difference between species.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Statistics argued against any biologically significant difference between species in shared root cell proportions.
source: The interindividual variability of the shared root cells was at a factor of >10 (range of 0.46–5.5% in macaque), and statistics argued against any biologically significant difference between species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis.

claim: A total of 13 cases (2 macaque, 11 human individuals) had percentages of shared root cells higher than percentages of AcD cells in Golgi material.
source: A total of 13 cases (2 macaque, 11 human individuals) had percentages of shared root cells higher than percentages of AcD cells, whereas in 22 of 25 individuals and/or cortical areas stained for biocytin and immunofluorescence the percentages of shared root cells were lower than the percentages of AcD cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: In 22 of 25 individuals and/or cortical areas stained for biocytin and immunofluorescence the percentages of shared root cells were lower than the percentages of AcD cells.
source: A total of 13 cases (2 macaque, 11 human individuals) had percentages of shared root cells higher than percentages of AcD cells, whereas in 22 of 25 individuals and/or cortical areas stained for biocytin and immunofluorescence the percentages of shared root cells were lower than the percentages of AcD cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The proportion of AcD neurons was slightly underrepresented in the Golgi material.
source: Thus, the proportion of AcD neurons was slightly underrepresented in the Golgi material.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of different staining methods.

claim: The biocytin material delivered significantly more shared root cells than immunofluorescence material.
source: Indeed, the biocytin material delivered significantly more shared root cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The unequivocal AcD cells were equally well recognized by both biocytin and immunofluorescence methods.
source: The unequivocal AcD cells were equally well recognized by both methods.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of different staining methods.

claim: Analysis of rat and ferret biocytin-stained pyramidal cells revealed that neither the dendrites sharing a root with an axon nor the AcDs had spine densities differing systematically from the spine density of non-AcDs from the very same neuron.
source: Analysis of rat and ferret biocytin-stained pyramidal cells, however, revealed that neither the dendrites sharing a root with an axon nor the AcDs had spine densities differing systematically from the spine density of non-AcDs from the very same neuron (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Kitten layer VI pyramidal cells showed adult percentages of AcDs early postnatally.
source: Kitten layer VI pyramidal cells (Figure 3A, Table 2) showed adult percentages of AcDs early postnatally.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3A and Table 2.

claim: Many pyramidal cells in kitten layer VI were L-shaped or inverted-fusiform, with the axon emerging from one of the dominant dendrites.
source: Many pyramidal cells were L-shaped or inverted-fusiform, with the axon emerging from one of the dominant dendrites (Lübke and Albus, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Infant macaque cortex exhibited percentages of AcD cells comparable to adult cortex neurons labeled with biocytin.
source: In line with this, infant macaque cortex exhibited percentages of AcD cells comparable to adult cortex neurons labeled with biocytin, and again, AcD cells were more frequent in infragranular layers (Figure 3A and B, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3A and B and Table 3.

claim: Of the pyramidal cells in kitten white matter, 43.31% had axons emerging from the major dendrite.
source: Unexpectedly, of the pyramidal cells in kitten white matter (Wahle et al., 1994), 43.31% had axons emerging from the major dendrite (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 2.

claim: 8.86% of the interstitial pyramidal neurons of the adult human white matter displayed AcDs.
source: Even more striking, 8.86% of the interstitial pyramidal neurons of the adult human white matter (Meyer et al., 1992) displayed AcDs (Table 4), and on average an additional 13.23% of the interstitial pyramidal cells had axons emerging from a shared root.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 4.

claim: On average an additional 13.23% of the interstitial pyramidal cells in adult human white matter had axons emerging from a shared root.
source: Even more striking, 8.86% of the interstitial pyramidal neurons of the adult human white matter (Meyer et al., 1992) displayed AcDs (Table 4), and on average an additional 13.23% of the interstitial pyramidal cells had axons emerging from a shared root.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 4.

claim: Up to 30% of the interneurons (all types pooled) in human cortex had an AcD.
source: Up to 30% of the interneurons (all types pooled) had an AcD (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: About 22% of Parvalbumin-positive neurons in human cortex had an AcD.
source: Furthermore, Parvalbumin-positive neurons were analyzed in immunostained human material. About 22% had an AcD (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Parvalbumin is a marker for gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic fast-spiking basket and chandelier cells.
source: Parvalbumin is a marker for gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic fast-spiking basket and chandelier cells, whereas neuropeptides are enriched in non-fast-spiking interneurons with Somatostatin being a marker for this interneuron lineage, at least in a rodent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about interneuron markers.

claim: Somatostatin is a marker for non-fast-spiking interneurons, at least in a rodent.
source: Parvalbumin is a marker for gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic fast-spiking basket and chandelier cells, whereas neuropeptides are enriched in non-fast-spiking interneurons with Somatostatin being a marker for this interneuron lineage, at least in a rodent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about interneuron markers.

claim: Somatostatin-positive neurons are GABA-ergic.
source: Somatostatin-positive neurons are GABA-ergic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about interneuron properties.

claim: About 12% of Neuropeptide Y-positive cells in kitten cortex had an AcD.
source: Neuropeptide Y-positive cells of mainly layers VI and V of the gray matter are often small basket neurons and also belong to the GABA-ergic neurons. About 12% had an AcD.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Neuropeptide Y-positive axonal loop cells of the cat subplate are a transient type of projection neuron.
source: Neuropeptide Y-positive axonal loop cells of the cat subplate are a transient type of projection neuron (Wahle and Meyer, 1987), which was recently reported to not contain glutamate decarboxylase (Ernst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only about 5% of Neuropeptide Y-positive axonal loop cells had an AcD.
source: Only about 5% had an AcD, the vast majority of axonal loop cells had the axon originating from the soma.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The vast majority of axonal loop cells had the axon originating from the soma.
source: Only about 5% had an AcD, the vast majority of axonal loop cells had the axon originating from the soma.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: For both neuropeptide Y-positive cell types, the proportion of AcD cells was constant through kitten postnatal development.
source: For both neuropeptide Y-positive cell types, this was constant through kitten postnatal development.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Of the Somatostatin-positive neurons 45–50% had an AcD.
source: Of the Somatostatin-positive neurons 45–50% had an AcD (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The apparent 'increase' in Somatostatin-positive AcD neurons early after birth rather reflected the differentiation of layer V/VI bitufted and Martinotti cells which begin to express Somatostatin more intensely.
source: It seems as if the percentage of Somatostatin-positive AcD neurons would increase early after birth. However, this 'increase' rather reflected the differentiation of layer V/VI bitufted and Martinotti cells which begin to express Somatostatin more intensely.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the developmental data.

claim: Somatostatin-positive AcD cells simply became easier to detect at higher numbers from P7-9 onward.
source: So, Somatostatin-positive AcD cells simply became easier to detect at higher numbers from P7-9 onward.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the developmental data.

claim: There are remarkable differences in AcD pyramidal neuron proportions between phylogenetic orders and position in gray and white matter.
source: Our data suggest remarkable differences between phylogenetic orders and position in gray and white matter.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical pyramidal neurons migrate radially upward while their axons emerge from the basal somatic pole and already during soma migration descend into the white matter.
source: Cortical pyramidal neurons migrate radially upward while their axons emerge from the basal somatic pole and already during soma migration descend into the white matter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal development.

claim: After the neurons have reached their laminar destination the leading process transforms into the apical dendrite, and basal dendrites begin to sprout.
source: After the neurons have reached their laminar destination the leading process transforms into the apical dendrite, and basal dendrites begin to sprout.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal development.

claim: It remains to be shown if, during basal dendritogenesis, the axon hillock becomes passively displaced from the soma onto an outgrowing dendrite.
source: It remains to be shown if, during basal dendritogenesis, the axon hillock becomes passively displaced from the soma onto an outgrowing dendrite.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism.

claim: The argument about passive displacement does not explain why the proportion of AcD neurons is much higher in hippocampus.
source: However, the argument does not explain why the proportion of AcD neurons is much higher in hippocampus although numbers published with intracellular labeling methods recently in rodent CA1 neurons vary from 20 (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020) to about 50% (Thome et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the proposed mechanism with observed data.

claim: Numbers published with intracellular labeling methods recently in rodent CA1 neurons vary from 20% to about 50%.
source: However, the argument does not explain why the proportion of AcD neurons is much higher in hippocampus although numbers published with intracellular labeling methods recently in rodent CA1 neurons vary from 20 (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020) to about 50% (Thome et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At this moment it is not clear if the axonal origin is always firmly anchored or can drift along the plasma membrane, for instance, by mechanical influences.
source: Furthermore, at this moment it is not clear if the axonal origin is always firmly anchored or can drift along the plasma membrane, for instance, by mechanical influences.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism.

claim: The AIS is a regulated microdomain which undergoes activity-dependent shifts in length and in position.
source: It is known that the AIS is a regulated microdomain (Jamann et al., 2018) which undergoes activity-dependent shifts in length and in position.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Dendrites are dynamic structures.
source: Dendrites are dynamic structures and although imaging studies in mouse have reported fairly stable basal dendrites of supragranular pyramidal neurons during development (Trachtenberg et al., 2002), there are also reports on dynamic changes elicited by environmental enrichment, activity, or disease (for review Hickmott and Ethell, 2006; Elston and Fujita, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Imaging studies in mouse have reported fairly stable basal dendrites of supragranular pyramidal neurons during development.
source: Dendrites are dynamic structures and although imaging studies in mouse have reported fairly stable basal dendrites of supragranular pyramidal neurons during development (Trachtenberg et al., 2002), there are also reports on dynamic changes elicited by environmental enrichment, activity, or disease (for review Hickmott and Ethell, 2006; Elston and Fujita, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There are reports on dynamic changes of dendrites elicited by environmental enrichment, activity, or disease.
source: Dendrites are dynamic structures and although imaging studies in mouse have reported fairly stable basal dendrites of supragranular pyramidal neurons during development (Trachtenberg et al., 2002), there are also reports on dynamic changes elicited by environmental enrichment, activity, or disease (for review Hickmott and Ethell, 2006; Elston and Fujita, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Domestic pig and wild boar had similar proportions of AcD neurons suggesting that domestication has no influence.
source: Domestic pig and wild boar had similar proportions suggesting that domestication has no influence.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of data from domestic pig and wild boar.

claim: Kitten and infant macaque data suggest that adult proportions of AcD neurons are already present at early ages.
source: Kitten and infant macaque data suggest that adult proportions of AcD neurons are already present at early ages, and the three assessments in infant macaque are within the macaque cluster (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the developmental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: In macaque, ontogenetically older infragranular pyramidal cells display more AcDs than later generated supragranular neurons.
source: In macaque, ontogenetically older infragranular pyramidal cells display more AcDs than later generated supragranular neurons, and the same was observed in our human material.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The same pattern of more AcDs in infragranular than supragranular neurons was observed in human material.
source: In macaque, ontogenetically older infragranular pyramidal cells display more AcDs than later generated supragranular neurons, and the same was observed in our human material.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: Neurons of the white matter seem to be a special case with respect to AcD proportions.
source: Neurons of the white matter seem to be a special case.

claim: In cat, the inverted pyramidal neurons represent a subset of subplate cells.
source: In cat, the inverted pyramidal neurons represent a subset of subplate cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cat cortical neurons.

claim: Subplate cells reside at strategic positions to monitor incoming inputs and may quickly relay that information to the overlying gray matter via axons ascending into the gray matter including layer IV.
source: They reside at strategic positions to monitor incoming inputs and may quickly relay that information to the overlying gray matter via axons ascending into the gray matter including layer IV (Friauf et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Subcortical afferents and white-to-gray matter projections match in topography.
source: Given that subcortical afferents and white-to-gray matter projections match in topography (reviewed by Molnár et al., 2020), a synaptic double-hit scenario has been postulated with geniculocortical afferents trying to strengthen synapses onto layer IV spiny stellates, and with excitatory subplate afferents transiently acting as 'helper synapse' and instructor for the developing thalamocortical connectivity (reviewed by Molnár et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A synaptic double-hit scenario has been postulated with geniculocortical afferents trying to strengthen synapses onto layer IV spiny stellates, and with excitatory subplate afferents transiently acting as 'helper synapse' and instructor for the developing thalamocortical connectivity.
source: Given that subcortical afferents and white-to-gray matter projections match in topography (reviewed by Molnár et al., 2020), a synaptic double-hit scenario has been postulated with geniculocortical afferents trying to strengthen synapses onto layer IV spiny stellates, and with excitatory subplate afferents transiently acting as 'helper synapse' and instructor for the developing thalamocortical connectivity (reviewed by Molnár et al., 2020).

claim: The findings suggest that action potential firing abilities bypassing somatic integration and somatic inhibition are advantageous during development of thalamocortical wiring.

claim: Adult human white matter pyramidal interstitial cells may differ from the transient subplate cells of non-primate cortex.

claim: Hamada et al., 2016 reported on neurons which by our criteria would not be AcD cells; their criterion for inclusion has been the distance of the spectrin/ankyrin G-labeled AIS to the soma irrespective of whether the axon emerges from a shared root or unequivocally from a dendrite.

claim: Considering a fraction of shared root will be tolerable, at least in non-primate mammals with their substantial numbers of unequivocal AcD neurons.
source: Together, considering a fraction of shared root will be tolerable, at least in non-primate mammals with their substantial numbers of unequivocal AcD neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of different criteria for defining AcD neurons.

claim: The human Golgi material yielded the lowest values of AcD and of AcD plus shared root cells.
source: The human Golgi material yielded the lowest values of AcD and of AcD plus shared root cells (Figure 5B) and the lowest proportion in supragranular layers (Figure 3B).

claim: The Golgi methods yielded a lower proportion of AcD neurons and the higher proportion of shared root cells.

claim: The Golgi reaction product is a chromate precipitate deposited at the plasma membrane.
source: The Golgi reaction product is a chromate precipitate deposited at the plasma membrane.

claim: The pitch-black reaction product, the thickness of the tissue sections, on top of the complexity of basal dendrites in primate and even more so in human can make it difficult to determine if an axon emerges from a soma, or from a shared root, or already from a very proximal dendritic trunk.

claim: With dark reaction products it was difficult to precisely determine where exactly a thin process lacking a clear hillock arises from a large dendritic root.
